activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: A 2001 study that observed children on school playgrounds found that other children were present during 88 percent of bullying episodes.
story:
The bus smelled like vinyl seats and wet raincoats, and Rosalie was halfway to her usual spot when she heard Dex's voice rise over the engine. "Milo thinks his bean plants are going to save the world," Dex was saying. "Future farmer of America, everybody." A couple of kids laughed. Milo stared at the notebook in his lap, where he'd been drawing diagrams for his agriculture project, rows and rows of little green sprouts labeled with careful arrows. Nobody said anything. That was the part Rosalie kept thinking about afterward, how everyone just sat there, herself included.

She slid into the seat across the aisle and pretended to dig through her backpack. Last month she had tried the direct route when Dex teased a sixth grader about her stutter. Rosalie had stood up in the cafeteria and shouted, "Leave her alone!" It had not gone well. The sixth grader got labeled as the girl who needed rescuing, Dex doubled down for a week, and Rosalie got a lecture from Mr. Okafor about causing a scene. She turned the moment over in her mind the way she turned a math problem, looking for where she'd gone wrong. Being loud wasn't the trouble, exactly. Being the only loud one was.

Then she remembered her brother's science fair poster from last spring, the one she'd read while eating popcorn in the gym. A study from 2001 had watched children on playgrounds and found that other children were present during 88 percent of bullying episodes. She'd thought it was a sad statistic then. Now, on the bus, it struck her differently. If other kids were almost always watching, then Dex was performing for an audience. Take the audience away, or turn it, and the whole thing might collapse. She looked down the aisle. Seven kids could hear this. Seven.

So she didn't stand up and she didn't shout. She leaned toward Milo and said, at a normal volume, "Hey, did your beans sprout yet? My grandma says you have to time it before the last frost." Milo's head came up. "They sprouted Tuesday," he said. "I've got fourteen." "Fourteen?" said Priya from two seats back. "Last year mine all drowned." "Mine too," admitted the kid by the window. "It rains too much in spring." Milo flipped his notebook around to show the diagram, and suddenly the aisle was full of bean talk, of failed gardens and one kid's uncle who grew pumpkins the size of beach balls.

Dex tried once more. "Boring," he announced, dragging the word out. But no one laughed this time, because everyone was busy arguing about drainage. Rosalie watched him glance around for a reaction that didn't come, and then he pulled out his phone and dismissed himself from the conversation entirely, earbuds in, invisible wall up. He wasn't punished or defeated. He just wasn't the show anymore.

Rosalie wasn't sure she'd done it right, or right enough. Maybe she should have said something straight to Dex, something assertive but calm, like her mom kept suggesting. Maybe tomorrow he'd pick on Milo again and she'd have to start over. The bus rattled over the pothole by the church, and Priya leaned across the aisle to ask Rosalie whether beans needed full sun. "Full sun," Milo answered for her, holding up the notebook page, one finger tapping the row marked Week Six, as the first sprouts of the drawing waved under the fluorescent light.

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: Babies under one year should be put to sleep on their backs, on a firm, flat surface with no pillows, blankets or toys, which lowers the risk of sudden infant death.
story:
Rose had babysat exactly one other child in her life, and that child had been seven and mostly interested in Minecraft, so holding four-month-old Daisy felt like being handed an emperor who ruled by screaming. The Willises had left a note on the fridge, and Rose had skimmed it while Daisy gummed her fist in the bouncy chair. "Back to sleep," the note said. "Firm flat mattress. Nothing in the crib. No pillows, blankets or toys." At the time it had seemed strange to her, because every picture she had ever seen of a baby showed a nest of soft things.

By seven o'clock Daisy was rubbing her eyes and fussing in that windup way Rose was starting to recognize. She carried the baby upstairs to the nursery, where a crib stood bare in the corner, just a tight fitted sheet on the mattress. On the rocking chair, though, someone had folded a fluffy yellow blanket with bunnies on it, clearly meant for a baby, clearly meant for this room.

Rose reached for it. Then she stopped, because the note had been underlined twice, and Mrs. Willis did not seem like a person who underlined things twice for no reason. The blanket was soft and warm and exactly what she would have wanted if she were the size of a loaf of bread. But babies under one year sleep on their backs, on a firm, flat surface, with nothing soft around them. That was the whole point of the empty crib, she realized. It was not unfinished. It was deliberate.

So she tested her idea the way she tested things: carefully, one step at a time. She laid Daisy on her back in the center of the firm mattress. Daisy screamed. Rose almost grabbed the bunny blanket right then, but instead she set the bouncy chair beside the crib where Daisy could see her face, and patted the baby's chest lightly and hummed the only song she knew all the words to, which was the theme from a cartoon. After a minute Daisy's fists unclenched. After three minutes her eyes closed.

Rose sat in the rocking chair with the yellow blanket folded on her knees, not daring to move it anywhere near the crib. When the Willises came home at nine, Mrs. Willis peeked into the nursery and then looked at Rose for a long moment.

"She's flat on her back," Rose whispered. "Nothing in the crib. I almost used the blanket, but your note, the underlines."

Mrs. Willis let out a breath like she'd been holding it since the front door. "Most sitters don't even read it. That blanket was a gift, and honestly I can't wait until she's old enough to use it."

"It's really soft," Rose said, still holding it, and Mrs. Willis laughed quietly and told her she was the permanent sitter now, if she wanted the job.

"Every Saturday?" Rose asked.

"Every Saturday," said Mrs. Willis. "I'll emphasize it to all the other parents at the park, too. The one who reads the notes." Down the hall, Daisy slept on her back, breathing in small even whispers, the empty crib steady around her like a promise Rose intended to keep.

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: Moving the horizon line up or down changes the view: a low horizon makes the street feel seen from a child's height, a high one from a window above.
story:
On the second Tuesday of art camp, Stella sat on the wooden porch of the crafts cabin, glaring at a page full of failed streets. Her buildings leaned like drunk fences, and her road refused to go anywhere. "Every line has to run toward the same point," her friend Marisol had said, tapping the dot she called the vanishing point, "the sides of the road, the rooftops, the windowsills, all of them." Stella had nodded, but her pencil had other plans.

That afternoon the counselor gave out a strange assignment. "Two drawings of the same street," she announced, "but from different spots. Stella, you take the curb. Marisol, the attic window of the main lodge." The lodge attic was rumored to hold an old trunk belonging to a camp artisan from the 1960s, someone who had painted every cabin sign by hand, and Marisol practically floated up the stairs to retrieve a look at it. Stella stayed below, sitting on the hot curb with her sketchbook balanced on her knees, pretending she was a spy watching a town full of secrets.

She drew the vanishing point first, right in the middle of the page, because that was where her eye landed when she stared down the dusty camp road. Then she let the road's edges race toward it. When she kept her pencil strokes parallel to the curb for the sidewalks, they looked wrong, so she angled them inward instead, toward the dot, and suddenly the road stretched away from her like a ribbon being pulled by a giant. The cabins shrank toward the point too. Her whole street looked like something seen by a small person standing right at the edge of things, close to the ground.

At the evening critique, the two drawings sat side by side, and Stella frowned. They showed the same road, the same cabins, the same crooked mailbox. Yet Marisol's street looked like it was seen from a window above, while Stella's felt like it was seen from a child's height, right down on the ground. Same street, same vanishing point rules. "Why do they look so different?" she asked the circle of campers.

Stella compared the pages again, hunting for the difference like a detective comparing fingerprints. Then she saw it. Her vanishing point sat low on the page. Marisol's sat high. "It's the horizon line," Stella said slowly. "Mine's down near the bottom because I was on the curb. Yours is way up because you were in the attic window." She slid the drawings together. "A low horizon makes the street feel seen from a child's height. A high one feels like you're looking from a window above."

The counselor said nothing, which was her way of saying Stella was right. Marisol grinned and flipped her paper over. "Draw the road again from my point of view," she dared. Stella set the vanishing point high, near the top, and watched her street climb the page like a kingdom seen from a castle tower. "Now make mine from the curb," Marisol said, holding out a fresh pencil.

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: In a healthy onion cell, the cell membrane is pressed tightly against the inside of the cell wall, which makes the membrane very hard to see as a separate line.
story:
Naomi had claimed the microscope in the farm's mudroom before anyone else could, because Grandpa kept his onions hanging in braids from the rafters and she needed one. She peeled a papery layer off a bulb, then teased a sliver of tissue from the inside of the fleshy ring, the part so thin it almost vanished against her fingertip. Under the lens, at forty times, the cells looked like pale bricks stacked in rows. At one hundred times, she could see the nucleus of each cell, a small dark circle floating in the middle like a seed. She drew the wall, the neat outer box of every brick, and the nucleus, and labeled both on her worksheet.

The third label, cell membrane, was the problem. She could not find it anywhere.

She adjusted the fine focus one click at a time, slowing down the way she did when she didn't want to miss something. The suspense made her mouth go dry. The wall was there. The nucleus was there. Between the wall and the inside of the cell, there was nothing, no second line, no gap, nothing to point to and label. Her cousin Theo leaned over from the window seat where he was supposed to be cataloging seeds.

"Maybe onions just don't have one," he said.

"They have to. It's on the sheet." She tapped the worksheet. "Every cell has a membrane. So it has to be somewhere in there."

"Then why can't you see it?"

Naomi didn't answer, because she was thinking about the wall itself. It was a thick, obvious line, easy to trace. She slid the slide a fraction to a cell that had been bent when she cut the tissue, one whose box was creased. In the crease, the wall folded inward, and pressed right along its inner edge was a fainter line, so close to the wall that it almost disappeared, thin as a breath. She held her breath too. There it was, hugging the inside of the wall.

"Look," she said, and Theo crossed the mudroom. She moved the slide back to a flat cell and let him look. "You can't see it here. In the healthy flat ones, the membrane is pressed so tightly against the inside of the cell wall that it's impossible to see as a separate line." She found another bent cell to prove it, tracing the faint line with her pencil point against the glass.

"So you label it on top of the wall?"

"I label it inside the wall." She drew a careful second line just within the first, touching it the whole way around, and wrote cell membrane beside it. Then she laughed, short and surprised. "The whole time it was hiding in the most obvious place."

Theo peered into the eyepiece one more time. "Bend me another cell," he said. "I want to see it too."

activity: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count
knowledge_domain: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count
fact: French political scientist Maurice Duverger observed that first-past-the-post elections tend to produce two large parties, an idea now called Duverger's law.
story:
Grandpa had a shoebox full of buttons, and he shook it like a maraca when Nevaeh walked in. "Election day," he said. "Grab the kitchen table."

He poured out the buttons and sorted them into four piles by color: red, blue, green, and yellow. Then he drew a map on a napkin, four squares side by side, and wrote numbers underneath. "In each square, one seat. Whoever's got the most buttons in that square wins it. Ready to count?" Nevaeh assumed the green pile, the biggest one, would clean up, because green had almost half of all the buttons in the box. But when they counted square by square, red and blue each took two seats, and green took none. In every single square, red and blue were just barely ahead.

"That's not fair," Nevaeh said, stacking the green buttons into a defeated little tower. "Green has the most buttons overall. How does green have zero seats?" She counted again, slower, because she wanted the first count to be wrong. It wasn't. In each square, green voters were split up so they lost everywhere by a hair. She tried moving five green buttons into one square, and green won that one, but lost the square she had taken them from. There was no arrangement where green came out ahead. She drummed her fingers. "So a party like this can only ever win by packing everyone together?"

Grandpa slid the napkin aside and drew a fresh one. "Now count it the other way. One big district, four seats, and the seats go out in proportion. Forty percent of the buttons, forty percent of the seats." Nevaeh did the math and sat back. Green got almost half the seats. Yellow, which had never come close in any square, still picked up one. Both systems used the same buttons, the same votes, and they built completely different parliaments. It was like discovering that the same recipe could make two different cakes depending on the pan.

"Why would anybody pick the first way, then?" she asked. Grandpa shrugged. "Some countries like governments that are durable, that last. Ask yourself what happens to green over time, if green keeps losing every square." Nevaeh thought about it. Green voters would stop wasting their vote, wouldn't they? They'd drift to red or blue, just to have a say. And green would shrink, election after election, until only the two big ones were left. "So the squares don't just pick winners," she said slowly. "They slowly erase everybody else."

"There's a name for that," Grandpa said. "Duverger's law. A French political scientist, Maurice Duverger, noticed that first-past-the-post elections tend to produce two large parties." Nevaeh wrote it on the corner of the napkin and put the napkin in her pocket. Her class was running a mock election next week, and for years the same two teams had traded the presidency back and forth like a family dynasty while three other parties got scraps. Nobody had ever asked why. She scooped the green buttons into her fist. "I'm bringing these to school on Monday."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Cutting an onion breaks its cells and releases enzymes that produce an irritating gas, which reaches the eyes and makes them water.
story:
Ellie set the cutting board on the picnic table at the back of the yard, where her mother's soup pot already sat bubbling over the little camp stove. Tonight was her turn to make dinner, and the recipe called for three onions, diced fine. Her little brother Marcus hovered nearby, hopping from foot to foot.

"I want to chop one," he said. "I'm not a baby anymore. I'm ten."

"You can chop the third one," Ellie said, "after I show you something." She halved the first onion and began cutting, and within a minute her eyes were stinging and streaming. Marcus watched her wipe her cheeks with her sleeve.

"You're crying because dinner's sad?" he asked.

"It's the onion," Ellie said, sniffling. "Cutting it breaks its cells and releases enzymes, and they produce an irritating gas. The gas reaches your eyes and makes them water." She had read that somewhere and half believed it, but reading a thing and living it were different. If the gas was the culprit, drifting up from the cut surfaces to her eyes, then putting a barrier between the onion and her eyes should stop the tears. She went inside and came back wearing her swim goggles. Marcus laughed so hard he had to sit down on the grass.

"Put them on and stop laughing," Ellie said. "Or are you too gullible to test a thing before you decide it's silly?" That got him. He marched over, took the second onion, and chopped it bare-faced, determined to prove the goggles were a joke. His eyes reddened, his nose ran, and tears rolled down while he kept insisting, voice wobbling, that he was fine. Then he snatched the goggles and chopped the last onion with his face sealed behind green plastic, and not one tear fell. He grinned like he'd won a prize.

"The goggles depict a very serious chef," Ellie said, handing him a wooden spoon so he could stir the pot while she added the onions. Steam rose, sweet and golden, and drifted toward the fence where the tenant from the garage apartment was grilling his own dinner. He leaned over and said it smelled better than his, and could he trade a piece of cornbread for a bowl later. Ellie agreed, because cornbread went perfectly with soup.

Marcus stirred in slow circles, still wearing the goggles. "Same time next week?" he asked. "I call goggles."

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: In 'The Wealth of Nations', published in 1776, Adam Smith pointed out that nothing is more useful than water, yet it will buy scarcely anything, while a diamond can buy a great deal.
story:
Mya had four dollars and one goal: a cold bottle of water before soccer practice. The gas station cooler held maybe a hundred bottles, all sweating in the air conditioning, priced at a dollar twenty-five. She grabbed one, then stopped. taped to the cooler door was a hand-written sign: "Bottled water now $1.25. Was 99 cents." She peeled the sign off to look at it, and the clerk behind the counter cleared his throat.

"Leave the sign, it's not decoration," he said. His name tag read DEV. "Owner raised it because we sell out every day. People want it, there's less of it, price goes up." He waved at the shelf of candy nobody bought. "Sour worms have been two-for-a-dollar since I started here. We got boxes of those in the back."

Mya put the sign back. She paid for her water and sat on the curb outside to drink it, because practice started in twenty minutes and the field was across the street. Her little brother Jaden was with her, kicking a pebble against the ice machine.

"Dev says water got expensive because everyone wants it," she told him.

"That's weird," Jaden said. He was eleven and treated every sentence as a challenge. "Water is the most important thing there is. It should cost the most. Way more than dumb stuff like diamonds. Why does a tiny diamond cost more than all the water in that cooler?"

Mya started to answer and found she had nothing. Water kept you alive; diamonds just sat there looking pointy. She took another drink and thought about the shelves inside. The candy nobody wanted was cheap. The water everybody wanted had just gotten pricier. So price followed wanting, not usefulness? That felt backwards, like being paid more for doing less.

"It's in my social studies book," she said slowly. "From last year. This guy Adam Smith wrote a whole book in 1776, The Wealth of Nations, and he talked about exactly this. He said nothing is more useful than water, yet water will buy scarcely anything, while a diamond can buy a great deal." She squinted at the parking lot, checking the sentence against the price tags she had just seen. "He noticed it two hundred years before Dev's boss raised the water a quarter."

"So is Jaden right or is Adam Smith right?" Jaden asked, which was not a real question.

"Smith. Obviously. He incorporated it into a whole book; you made it up on a curb." A delivery truck pulled in then, and a driver got out hauling two more full racks of water bottles, which meant the station's supply was about to be plentiful again. Mya stood, brushed off her shorts, and pointed at the truck. "Watch. Bet the price drops back once they've got stacks of it nobody has to fight over. The gas station's whole revenue probably depends on people like me panic-buying water at a dollar twenty-five, and I resent being part of that."

"You paid it," Jaden said.

"I was thirsty. That's a distinct problem from being wrong."

Dev came out to sign for the delivery, read his clipboard, and laughed. "Tell your brother," he called over the truck's engine, "water's back to 99 cents on Friday."

Mya held up her half-empty bottle like a trophy. "Jaden. Friday. Bring your allowance."

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
knowledge_domain: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
fact: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.4 degrees from straight up relative to the plane of its orbit around the Sun.
story:
Matteo stood at the edge of the old quarry and looked down at the flooded pit, where the water refracted the afternoon light into broken green ribbons. He had a problem, and it was due tomorrow: Mr. Okoye had assigned him to explain the seasons, and Matteo still did not understand why summer happened. His friend Dara was sure it was because Earth got closer to the Sun in June, and Matteo had believed her for two whole weeks.

"Not the distance," Matteo said now, holding up the library globe he had lugged out here on the bus. "The librarian said Earth is actually closest to the Sun during northern winter. So distance can't be it."

"Then what?" Dara said. She set her flashlight on a stable flat rock so it wouldn't roll, pointing it at the globe like a tiny Sun.

Matteo spun the globe and noticed something he had never paid attention to before. "Look," he said, tilting his head. "It's leaning." The metal axis, the bar running from pole to pole, wasn't straight up and down the way he'd always drawn Earth in his notes. He checked it against the plumb line the quarry workers had left hanging from a post, a string with a bolt tied to the end. The line hung perfectly vertical. The globe's axis did not match it.

He borrowed Dara's protractor and measured. "About twenty-three point four degrees," he said, "from straight up." Then he remembered the diagram in the library book, the one showing Earth's path around the Sun. The axis leaned compared to that flat ring of the orbit, and it leaned the same way the whole way around, like a spinning top that never wobbles over.

"Watch this," Matteo said. He stood the flashlight in for the Sun and walked the globe around it in a slow circle, keeping the axis tipped the same direction each step. When the North Pole tipped toward the flashlight, his half of the globe caught the light straight on, bright and concentrated. Halfway around, the North Pole tipped away, and the same light spread thin and slanted across the north. He held his hand where the light hit. It was warmer when the light came straight down.

"That's it," Dara said slowly. "It's the tilt. Same light, different angle." She frowned at her own notebook, where she had written distance in big letters. "I'm changing my answer."

"Me too," Matteo said. He turned the globe once more around the steady beam, the little tilted Earth crossing the dark water's shine, and did not stop smiling the whole way around.

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: Dutch army surgeon Antonius Mathijsen developed the plaster-of-Paris bandage for setting broken bones and published his method in 1852.
story:
Piper sat on the swings without swinging, her left arm sticking out of a bright green cast, and watched everyone else race across the playground. Two days ago she had been reckless, jumping off the top of the slide to prove she could land like a cat, and now the whole class had opinions about her cast. Most of them were about the color.

"Green is the worst," said Marcus, dropping onto the swing beside her. "You should have gotten blue." He turned his own arm over, as if comparing it to an invisible blue one. "Hey, how did people even keep broken bones still before they had casts? Did they just lie around for a year?"

Piper hadn't thought about that. She looked down at the hard green shell on her arm, the signatures already crowding the surface, and wondered. Somebody had to be the first person to wrap a broken arm in this stuff. Maybe a doctor, somewhere, long ago. "I don't know," she said. "But I can find out before class tomorrow."

The library computer gave her the answer faster than she expected. She scribbled it on a napkin at dinner and read it three times so she wouldn't get it wrong. Dutch army surgeon Antonius Mathijsen developed the plaster-of-Paris bandage for setting broken bones and published his method in 1852. An army surgeon. That part made sense to Piper, actually; soldiers probably broke a lot of bones. She kept turning the date over in her head while she ate, thinking that 1852 was a long, long time before her grandmother was even born.

The next morning at recess, Marcus found her by the fence. "So? Did you evaluate the situation, or what?"

Piper laughed. "I looked it up. A Dutch army surgeon named Antonius Mathijsen developed the plaster-of-Paris bandage, for setting broken bones, and he published his method in 1852."

"Plaster of Paris," Marcus repeated slowly, like tasting the words. "So this whole time I've been signed by everybody on a plaster-of-Paris bandage."

"You're standing on a jury of one," Piper said, pointing at his face, "and the jury finds the cast not guilty of being ugly." Marcus made a face at her, but he signed it too, right under the bubble letters that said GET WELL SOON, CAT.

By the end of recess the cast was nearly full, and Piper ran her thumb over the drying ink, over the name of a girl who had jumped and a line about a surgeon she'd never meet. Marcus asked if she'd jump off the slide again. She said maybe, someday, with a helmet, and he shook his head and pushed off on his swing, pumping higher.

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
knowledge_domain: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
fact: In James Hurst's 1960 story The Scarlet Ibis, a storm-blown red bird dies in the family garden, foreshadowing the fate of the fragile boy Doodle.
story:
Ava slid The Scarlet Ibis across the library table like it might bite her. "Mr. Ruiz wants a paragraph on foreshadowing by Friday," she told her friend Marcus, who was balancing a pencil on his nose. "He says the story is full of clues, and I can't find a single one."

Marcus dropped the pencil. "Clues in a story about a bird? That's bizarre. It's not a mystery."

"That's what I said." Ava flopped the book open to the page where a red bird, exhausted and storm-tossed, tumbles out of the tree into the family garden and dies. She tapped the paragraph. "See? Big red bird, weird weather, drops dead in the yard. And the little brother, Doodle, he's the fragile one, always tired, always behind. It felt strange when I read it, like the story was winking at me."

"So it's a clue?" Marcus leaned over her shoulder, breathing cheese crackers into her airspace.

"I think the bird's death corresponds to something later," Ava said slowly, turning pages. "Like a shadow falling before the thing that casts it." She found the ending, where Doodle, fragile Doodle, dies in the storm. She sat back so fast her chair squeaked. "The bird dies in the garden in a storm. Doodle dies in a storm. The bird was showing me what was coming, pages before it happened. That's what foreshadowing is! The story told me the future and I missed it!"

Marcus picked up his pencil and pointed it at her like a wand. "Ava Mercado, story detective."

"Shhh." The librarian glared from behind the desk, and Ava lowered her voice. "Okay, so here's my test. If the bird is a clue, then it should match Doodle in more ways than one. The bird is red. Doodle, when he dies, is red too. Red all over. I read that part three times because it wouldn't let go of me." She pulled her notebook over and began writing, her pencil scratching fast. "So the bird isn't just a bird. It stands for Doodle. There's a word for that too, Mr. Ruiz said it last week." She flipped back through her notes, past a doodle of a dinosaur wearing glasses, and found it. "Symbolism. The bird is a symbol."

"Like when I call you a dictionary," Marcus said, "but nicer."

"Exactly like that, but with a bird." Ava wrote her topic sentence, crossed it out, wrote a better one. "Paragraph: the scarlet ibis dying in the garden is foreshadowing because it comes before Doodle's death and matches it, and it's also a symbol, because the red, tired bird stands for the fragile boy. And I can prove it with quotes." She stacked her pages with a satisfying smack, like a judge closing a case.

Marcus saluted her with the pencil. "Detective Dictionary, the story never stood a chance."

Ava checked out the book, hugged it to her chest, and marched for the door. "Friday's going down."

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: VisiCalc, written by Dan Bricklin and Bob Frankston and released for the Apple II in 1979, was the first spreadsheet program for personal computers.
story:
Chase slid into the seat at the library computer next to the window, where the afternoon light hit the keyboard just right. He had exactly one hour before his mom picked him up, and one mission: prove he had saved two hundred dollars from dog walking so his parents would cover the rest of the new bike. He opened the spreadsheet program, typed "Date" in the first column and "Money" in the second, and started entering every job from his notebook, all the way back to March.

The librarian, Ms. Reyes, leaned over the desk nearby. "You look like a man with a plan."

"A bike plan," Chase said. "I need a formula that adds the whole column."

She showed him once, typing "=SUM(" and letting him finish. When he pressed Enter, a number appeared at the bottom of the column, and it was wrong. It said one hundred sixty-two dollars, and Chase knew, knew, he had more than that. He'd counted the cash in the shoebox twice.

Here is what he remembered then, standing there with his hand on the mouse. Last summer, his grandpa had visited and sat with him on the porch, and when Chase complained about math homework, Grandpa laughed so hard he nearly spilled his tea. "You think that's hard? When I was young, we did sums by hand, rows and rows of them. Then VisiCalc came out. Dan Bricklin and Bob Frankston wrote it, and it was the first spreadsheet program for personal computers. Ran on the Apple II, back in 1979. I remember seeing it on a friend's machine and thinking the future had arrived in a living room." He had tapped Chase's notebook. "The beauty of it was, you change one number, and everything recalculates. No erasing."

So Chase reasoned the same thing had to work in reverse. If the total was wrong, something in the column had to be wrong, even if he couldn't see it yet. The sum was like a detective that never lied. He decided to test it, the way Grandpa would have. He made a new column and typed his numbers again, slowly, watching the running total evaluate after each one, climbing like a thermometer. Twelve dollars, twenty-eight, forty-one. Then he hit a row where the total didn't move at all. He had typed the eleven dollars from the Hendersons' poodle without a dollar sign, and the program had treated it like a word, not a number. Hidden, sneaky, invisible until the total gave it away.

"Ha!" he said, loud enough that a boy at the next computer looked over. "Sorry," Chase whispered, but he was grinning. He fixed the cell, and the total jumped to two hundred nineteen dollars. Then he highlighted the whole column and clicked the chart button, and bars rose up across the screen like a tiny city, April tall and proud, June taller. The Hendersons' bar would have been missing entirely, a gap in the skyline, if he hadn't caught it.

Ms. Reyes walked by again and studied the chart. "Nice. What's it for?"

"Bike evidence," Chase said. "For the parents."

"That's smart," she said. "Though I'll warn you, eleven-year-old savings can be volatile. One trip to the game store and the whole chart collapses."

"That's why it's in a shoebox at home," Chase said. "The money doesn't know about the game store."

He was printing the chart, two copies because his mom liked to keep one on the fridge, when a thought struck him and he laughed out loud again. Grandpa had told him spreadsheets were invented in 1979, and here Chase was making one, and somewhere along the way he had almost lost eleven dollars to a typo the exact same way people must have lost money for forty years. When his mom came in, he held up the warm pages and pointed at the tallest bar.

"That's June," he said. "June was a very good month for dogs."

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Two-factor authentication asks for a second proof, such as a code sent to your phone, so a stolen password alone is not enough to get into an account.
story:
Felix's new phone buzzed in his hand for the very first time, and he nearly dropped it on the kitchen table. The screen glowed with his first message, a text from his older sister Rosa: "Welcome to civilian phone life, weirdo. Now you can actually answer texts instead of staring at mine like an anonymous ghost." He laughed out loud. Twelve years old, and finally a phone owner. He had big plans: a group chat, photos of his dog Biscuit, and a messaging app where his friends were already arguing about the school talent show.

He was halfway through setting up his account when the phone buzzed again. A number he didn't know had sent a code: "Your login verification code is 4912." Felix frowned. He hadn't asked for any code. He read it twice, then a third time, his heart starting to thump. If he hadn't requested a code, then somebody else had. And the only reason a stranger would request a code for his account was that the stranger already knew his password.

"Rosa," he called toward the stairs. "If you get a code you never asked for, what does that mean?"

Rosa appeared in the doorway, chewing the end of a pen. "Dad calls that two-factor authentication," she said. "The code is a second proof, like a key plus a knock. A stolen password alone doesn't get anyone in, because they still need the code sent to your phone." She pointed at his screen. "So who's knocking?"

Felix's mind raced. He hadn't shared his password with anyone, except once, three days ago, when he'd borrowed Marcus's laptop at the library and typed it in to show him a video. He grabbed his phone and typed fast: "Marcus, did you save my password on your laptop?" The reply came in seconds, a sheepish message: "My cousin's been using my laptop all weekend. I didn't think about it. Sorry."

"So some anonymous person on Marcus's laptop has my password," Felix said. He didn't panic. Instead he tested his idea, the way he'd test a science hypothesis. He changed his password first, then watched the phone. No more mystery codes. Nothing arrived all evening. The hidden cause was gone, and the evidence proved it.

"Rosa! No new codes since I changed it!" he shouted, and she thumped down the stairs to see for herself.

"Nice work," she said. Then she grinned. "Group chat. Now. And don't you dare abandon us for your dog photos."

Felix opened the new chat and typed the first message: "Felix has entered civilian life. Biscuit photos begin in five minutes."

activity: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
knowledge_domain: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
fact: Most traditional bar soaps are basic, with a pH of around 9 to 10.
story:
Florence flattened the crumpled note on the kitchen table and read it again. "Dear Sherlock," her grandmother had written, "the science kit you left here says to test things with the special paper. I have no idea how to participate in chemistry, but I have vinegar, lemon juice, and the soap by my sink. Bring yourpH paper Sunday. Love, Gran."

Florence had exactly two days to figure out how the strips worked before she had to look smart in Gran's kitchen. On Saturday morning she laid out her supplies on the counter: a small vial of blue litmus paper, a red strip from the same package, and a row of cups. In the first cup she splashed vinegar. In the second she squeezed a lemon. In the third she mixed a pinch of baking soda into water until it turned translucent and shimmery at the top.

She dipped a blue strip into the vinegar and held her breath. The paper flushed pink, then red. She tried the lemon juice, and the same thing happened. When she dipped blue paper into the baking soda cup, nothing changed, but the red strip she poked in afterward turned a deep, stubborn blue. Florence grinned. It was like the paper had two teams, and each strip could only cheer for the side it wasn't already on. She drew a wobbly scale in her notebook, acids on one end, bases on the other, and labeled every cup.

On Sunday she carried her notebook into Gran's kitchen like a detective carrying evidence. "Okay, Gran, hold out your hand." Gran held out the hand with her wedding ring, a pale gold alloy worn thin on one side. "First the vinegar," Florence said, and touched a wet blue strip to Gran's fingertip. It went red. "Acid. Now the soapy water." Gran turned on the tap and worked up a lather over the bar of soap by the sink. Florence dipped the strip and stared. The paper stayed blue. She dipped again, sure she had done it wrong, and then pressed a red strip into the bubbles instead. It turned blue, bright and unmistakable.

"That's the soap being basic," Florence said. "Most traditional bar soaps are basic, around a pH of 9 to 10, so it's on the opposite side of the scale from your vinegar." She checked her notebook scale and slid her finger from the acid end all the way across.

Gran peered at the blue strip over her glasses. "So I've been washing my dishes with the enemy of my salad dressing." She held the strip up to the window light, then tucked it carefully into the pocket of her apron. "I'm keeping this one. Proof that I participated in a real experiment."

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: Studies show that nearsightedness is less common in people who spent more time outdoors during childhood.
story:
The nurse's office smelled like bandages and orange juice, and Grace sat on the crinkly paper of the cot while Nurse Alvarez read a note from the eye doctor. The walls had a poster of a food pyramid and a crooked door that swung on one hinge whenever anyone came in. Grace's new glasses sat in a blue case on her lap, and she had been postponing the moment when she would open it, because once she put them on, everything would be different.

"Dr. Osei says you can wear them full time or just for the board," Nurse Alvarez said. "Your call, mostly."

Grace opened the case. The frames were purple, smaller than she expected. When she slid them on, the room snapped into focus so sharply that she blinked. She could read the tiny label on the thermometer across the office. She could see the individual squares in the ceiling tiles. She turned to the door, watching its loose hinge swing, and thought about how she had never noticed it was broken before, even though she had been in this room a dozen times.

"Everything so blurry before, and I didn't even know," she said.

"That's usually how it goes," Nurse Alvarez said. "You think the whole world sees it that way."

Grace's little brother, Marcus, was the reason she was here at all. He had an appointment with Dr. Osei next month, and Grace had overheard her mom worrying that Marcus would need glasses too. Grace had spent the whole weekend indoors, first at Marcus's side while he played games on his tablet, then on her own phone until her eyes ached. At the eye doctor's office yesterday, she had heard something that stuck in her head. There was a poster in the waiting room that said nearsightedness is less common in people who spent more time outdoors during childhood. Dr. Osei had even said it out loud to a boy in the next chair, a boy who admitted he never went outside on weekends. Less common. Not impossible, she knew that, but less common.

She thought about testing it. Marcus was seven, still in his childhood years, whatever those counted as. If the rule was real, then getting him outside more might actually matter, and it would be negligent of her to keep modeling weekends on the couch. So she made a plan on the spot: Saturday, she would take him to the creek path behind the library, before he could even find his tablet.

She stood up and folded the note into her pocket. "Can I take an extra brochure about eyes?" she asked. "For my brother."

Nurse Alvarez pulled one from the drawer and held it out. "He'll listen to a girl in new glasses," she said.

Grace put it in her backpack next to her library card and pushed through the door, listening to the hinge squeak behind her all the way down the hall.

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: Washington's Zackery Lystedt Law, passed in 2009, was the first U.S. state law requiring that a young athlete with a suspected concussion be removed from play until a health professional clears them.
story:
Theo was on his fourth lap of the rink when he noticed that Marcus, the fastest skater at tryouts, had started drifting toward the boards on every turn. That was strange. Marcus never drifted. Two minutes ago Marcus had gone into the corner hard, and though Theo hadn't seen the collision itself, he had heard the dull thunk of helmet against ice when Marcus went down.

"You okay?" Theo asked, gliding up beside him during the water break.

"Fine," Marcus said. "Just dizzy for a second. Coach already called it, anyway. I've got to show them I can play."

Theo studied him. Marcus's eyes looked slow, like they were arriving at things a beat late. When the coach blew the whistle for the passing drill, Marcus raised his left hand to catch a pass aimed at his right. Theo skated closer. There was a pattern here, something invisible underneath the "I'm fine," and Theo wanted to test it before it got worse.

"Hey, do this," Theo said, and he mimicked the coach's warm-up routine, touching his right glove to his left shoulder, then switching, quick and even.

Marcus tried it. His gloves got tangled, and he touched the same shoulder twice. The second time, he grimaced and pressed a palm against his temple.

"That's it," Theo said, and he waved the coach over. "I think he hit his head."

"He told me he was fine," the coach said, but she pulled Marcus off the ice anyway. "Washington's Zackery Lystedt Law. Passed in 2009, first state law like it in the country. Any young athlete with a suspected concussion comes out of play until a health professional clears him."

"So it's not your choice?" Theo asked.

"Or his," the coach said, steering Marcus toward the bench. "That's the point."

Theo sat beside Marcus while they waited for his mom, the cold leaking through his socks, the smell of burnt coffee and stale popcorn drifting from the lobby. He remembered being nine, at a summer camp, when he had kept swimming after whacking his chin on the diving board because he didn't want to sit out in front of everyone. He'd told the counselor he was fine, and the counselor, who was seventeen and reckless about everything except sunscreen, had believed him. Theo still wasn't sure whether keeping going had been brave or just dumb.

"Can I try out again?" Marcus asked the coach, his voice small.

"When a doctor clears you," she said. "Tryouts run two weeks. You might miss your chance, and I'm sorry about that."

Marcus stared at his skates. "I lied," he said finally. "About being fine."

"I know," Theo said. "Your gloves told on you."

Marcus almost laughed, then grabbed his head with both hands, and Theo went to get the ice pack.

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: A spreadsheet cell's address is its column letter followed by its row number, so C4 is the cell in column C, row 4.
story:
Isla had missed two days of school with a cold, and now the spreadsheet project was due on Friday. Mr. Delgado's rubric said the spreadsheet had to add up a column of numbers with a formula and then turn the numbers into a bar chart. Isla's data was still in her friend Priya's notebook, and Priya was reading it to her over the phone.

The data was from the sixth-grade bake sale. Every row was one table, and every table had counted its cupcake money. "Table one, eighteen dollars," Priya read. "Table two, twenty-four. Table three, thirty-one." Isla typed each number into a column and watched it stack up, gray line after gray line.

Then Priya said, "Okay, I found the total for table four. It's in C4. Forty dollars."

Isla typed forty into the wrong place, and her column looked lopsided. She squinted at the screen. Somewhere in the back of her mind a rule was trying to surface, the way the answer to a math problem sometimes arrives before you finish writing the problem. She clicked on a cell at random and watched the little box at the top of the screen. When she clicked the cell in column C, row 4, the box said C4. When she clicked the cell in column C, row 5, it said C5. The letter came first, then the number. So C4 was the cell in column C, row 4, and if Priya had said "row four" instead of just a number, Isla would have known exactly where to look.

"You read me forty from C4," she said into the phone, "but I put it in row six. My whole column is wrong now."

"That's not my fault," Priya said. "Your notebook is a mess. Half these numbers look like they inherited their handwriting from your older brother."

Isla fixed the column, then built her formula. She clicked the empty cell below her numbers, typed the equals sign, and summed everything from the first cell to the last. When she pressed Enter, the total appeared at once: one hundred fifty-three dollars. The number sat there looking credible, like it had always known the answer and was only waiting to be asked.

The bar chart took two more clicks. Five bars rose up out of the data, table three tallest, table five embarrassingly short. Isla titled it "Bake Sale by Table," sat back with a tissue, and said, "Friday, we are ready for you."

"That's not a very scary audition," Priya said.

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
knowledge_domain: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
fact: Stress can show up in the body as headaches, a tight or upset stomach, sweaty palms or trouble falling asleep.
story:
Muhammad wanted the rope bridge more than anything at Camp Whitfield. The crossing counted toward the Junior Trailblazer badge, and everyone in his cabin had already signed up for Friday. But on Thursday night he lay on his bunk under the canvas canopy of the tent, wide awake, listening to Danish snoring two feet away. His stomach felt tight and sour, and when he finally did drift off, he dreamed the bridge had no ropes at all.

At breakfast he barely touched his pancakes. His head ached in a dull band across his forehead, and when the unit leader called names for the morning swim, his palms were so sweaty that the pencil slipped out of his hand twice. Danish frowned at him. "You look like you swallowed a wasp." Muhammad shrugged and said he was fine, because if he said otherwise, someone might decide he was too sick for Friday.

The camp nurse, Ms. Farah, had a small office near the dining hall, and Muhammad ended up there anyway after his stomach acted up again at lunch. She felt his forehead, looked in his ears, and asked normal questions. Then she leaned back and asked one that seemed strange. "Is anything big happening tomorrow?" Muhammad blinked. "The rope bridge," he said slowly. "I signed up for it." She nodded as if that settled the matter, and wrote something on a card. "Stress can show up in the body as headaches, a tight or upset stomach, sweaty palms, or trouble falling asleep," she said. "It doesn't mean you're sick. It means your body is talking."

Muhammad stared at the card in his hand. He thought about Sunday nights at home, when his stomach used to knot up before Monday math quizzes, and how his mother had always blamed the canteen food. He had never once connected the two. The pattern was invisible, but there it was, plain as a trail marker, and he wanted to test it. "So if I calm my body down, the stomachache stops?" Ms. Farah smiled. "That's an experiment worth running."

He ran it that afternoon. Sitting on a flat rock behind the arts shed, where ferns flourished in the damp shade, he breathed the way the card showed: in for four counts, hold, out slow. He did it until his palms dried and the tightness in his stomach loosened like a knot working itself undone. That night he followed the sleep routine Ms. Farah had jotted down, no flashlight games with Danish, just the same three slow stretches and the same slow breathing in his sleeping bag. He was asleep before the crickets got loud.

Friday morning came bright and cool. Muhammad stood at the base of the rope bridge with his harness clipped and his heart hammering, and for a second the sour feeling crept back toward his stomach. He breathed, in for four, out slow, right there where everyone could see him. Then he took the first plank. The bridge swayed, the river glittered far below, and Danish yelled something from the far platform. Halfway across, Muhammad realized he had forgotten to be scared at all. "Come on, slowpoke!" Danish shouted. Muhammad grinned and took the next plank.

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: The phone Martin Cooper used for the first handheld cell phone call weighed about 1.1 kilograms (2.5 pounds).
story:
Tyler sat near the window with the box in his backpack, and every time the bus bounced over a pothole he checked that the box was still there. His parents had finally decided to permit him a phone of his own, but only after he signed a list of rules on the fridge, all eleven of them. Rule six said the phone came to school but stayed in the backpack during class. Rule nine said he had to answer when his mom called. He had read the list three times at the kitchen table while his grandfather laughed and picked up the little phone, weighing it in one hand.

"Light as a biscuit," Grandpa said. "The first handheld cell phone call ever made, the man who made it, Martin Cooper, that phone weighed about one point one kilograms. Two and a half pounds." He handed it back to Tyler. "A kilogram and a bit. Like carrying a bag of sugar."

Tyler hadn't believed it at first. He had held the new phone in one palm and thought about the bag of sugar in the pantry, which was one kilogram, and his grandfather's number had to be right on top of that. Now, on the bus, he wanted to test it. In his backpack he had his history textbook, which the librarian had told him weighed one kilogram, because students always asked. He slid the book out, balanced the phone on top of it, and lifted both together. His hand dropped a little under the book alone. The phone was almost nothing.

"Are you weighing your phone with a textbook?" said Desmond, dropping into the seat across the aisle. Desmond was notorious for noticing everything, which was sometimes fun and sometimes not.

"Sort of an experiment," Tyler said. "My grandpa says the first handheld cell phone, the one Martin Cooper used for the first call, weighed about one point one kilograms. Two and a half pounds. Mine is way lighter than the book, and the book is one kilogram." He stacked them again, then held the book low and the phone high. "See? There's no comparison."

Desmond squinted at the little tower of phone and book. "So the first one weighed like a whole textbook plus some?"

"About that."

"That would wreck your pocket," Desmond said, and Tyler laughed and put the book away. Outside the window the fence posts went by in an even rhythm, and he felt the phone's thin weight through the canvas of the backpack, still exactly where he'd left it.

At his stop he climbed down the steps and patted the side pocket once. "Two and a half pounds," he said to himself, and walked up the drive.

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: Gold was discovered at Sutter's Mill in California in January 1848, starting the California Gold Rush that drew people west in huge numbers.
story:
Colton pressed his nose close to the glass case in the history museum's westward expansion room. Inside lay a leather diary with cracked corners, open to a page written in spidery brown ink. His worksheet asked one question: use a primary source to explain why people moved west in the 1800s. He had exactly twenty minutes before his class regrouped at the entrance, and he had nothing written yet.

He read the first line under his breath. "April the 3rd, 1848. We crossed the river today, and Josiah will not stop talking of California." Colton glanced at the little plaque beside the case. The diary had belonged to a settler named Emmett Hall, traveling with his brother. He copied the line down, but it didn't answer anything. Why California? The word "gold" appeared on the next page, and Colton's instinct told him there was a story behind it.

He went back to the beginning and worked through the pages in a systematic way, line by line, the way his science teacher had shown him for checking data. The entries from early 1848 talked about farmland and a fresh start. Then, halfway through April, the tone changed. "News reached our camp tonight," Emmett had written. "Gold was discovered at Sutter's Mill in California in January of this year. They say men are pulling nuggets from the river with their hands."

Colton's pencil stopped. January 1848. That was months before Emmett even wrote about it. He turned to his friend Dana, who was squinting at a map on the far wall. "Hey, Dana. Gold was discovered at Sutter's Mill in California in January 1848," he said. "That's what started the whole Gold Rush. Look at the date on this diary."

Dana came over, and they bent over the case together. The next entry made Colton's stomach drop. "Josiah has left us. He took the mule and headed for the mill. I am staying on to the valley, for I came for land, not for gold." Colton had assumed everyone in these wagons wanted the same thing, but the diary was splitting them apart right in front of him. Some travelers came for farmland, and some came for money, pulled west by a discovery made before they even left home.

He filled two lines on his worksheet, then paused. One more page remained, and the ink there looked darker, newer. "October. A letter found me at last. Josiah writes from the mill. He has found little gold, but he has work weighing sacks for the miners, and he says the ground hums like a beehive. He asks me to save him a plot of land beside mine." Colton read it twice. The brother who had bolted for riches was now asking for exactly what Emmett had wanted all along.

Dana pointed at the final line of the diary. "Does it say what Emmett answered?"

Colton leaned closer. The last entry, dated a week later, read: "I have driven the fence posts to mark his half. He is my brother, and the valley has room."

"He saved it," Colton said quietly, still staring at the fence posts he would never see.

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
knowledge_domain: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
fact: To change a speed in meters per second into kilometers per hour, multiply it by 3.6.
story:
Nicolas skidded to a stop in front of the Rolling Race exhibit, where a long ramp curved down into a timing track. A basket of balls sat beside it, and a sign said: Measure distance. Measure time. Graph it. He grabbed a stopwatch from the bin, plucked out a bright orange ball, and turned to the kid already standing there, a girl with a clipboard and a pencil behind her ear.

"I bet my ball rolls faster than a person walks," Nicolas said. "Fast walking is about six kilometers per hour."

"Then you'd better measure," said the girl, whose name turned out to be Priya. She pointed to the marks on the track. "Every stripe is half a meter, and the counter shows seconds." They set the orange ball at the top of the ramp, and Priya counted down. "Three, two, one, go." The ball zipped down and crossed the three meter mark while the stopwatch read 1.4 seconds. Nicolas wrote the numbers on the back of his hand, then ran it again, because one try could be a fluke, and again. Three meters, always close to 1.4 seconds.

He worked the division on the edge of Priya's clipboard. "Three divided by 1.4 is about 2.1 meters per second. But walking speed is in kilometers per hour, not meters per second. How do you compare those?"

Priya tapped the panel on the exhibit wall, and there it was, printed under the title The Conversion Principle: to change a speed in meters per second into kilometers per hour, multiply it by 3.6. Nicolas read it twice, then multiplied. "2.1 times 3.6 is about 7.6 kilometers per hour!" He leapt sideways out of the way of a toddler chasing a big buoyant foam ball that had bounced off the ramp. "Priya. PRIYA. That beats fast walking."

"It does," Priya said, already ruling lines on graph paper. "Now draw it. Distance on this side, time along the bottom." Nicolas plotted the three runs, and the dots climbed in a straight, stubborn line. "It's straight," he said. "Same slope every time. The ball doesn't slow down on the flat track, so the speed stays the same, and same speed means a straight line." Priya added one more point from a slow, heavy rubber ball she rolled herself, and its line lay flatter, like a hill tilted gently down.

"Yours is steeper," she said. "Steep line, fast ball." Nicolas stared at the two lines crossing his graph like roads, then flipped his stopwatch over and over in his hand. "Okay. New goal. Seven point six is good, but a sprinter does twenty kilometers per hour." He sprinted to the basket, dug all the way to the bottom, and came up holding a dense steel ball bearing. "You time," he said, already climbing to the top of the ramp.

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: On a standard 400-metre outdoor track, the 800 metres is exactly two laps, so runners plan the race as a first lap and a second lap.
story:
The basketball court behind the middle school had been chalked off into a rough oval that spring, because Coach Reyes liked his runners to practice somewhere with fences and cracks and obstacles, something a smooth track never offered. Ethan stood at the painted start line with six other boys, and Coach walked the curve with a clipboard, taking a quick census of who was racing the eight hundred and who had signed up for the sprints. Ethan raised his hand.

"The eight hundred is exactly two laps," Coach said, tapping the chalk oval. "On a four-hundred-metre track, two laps, that's the whole race. First lap, second lap. Nothing else." Then he blew the whistle before anyone could ask more.

Ethan had a plan, and the plan was simple: hold back on the first lap so his legs still worked on the second. The trouble was the boy next to him, a tall kid named Marcus from another school who wore mismatched shoes and ran with a flailing, eccentric arm swing that made him look like he was swatting bees. Marcus shot off the line like the race was twenty metres long. Ethan let him go, counting his own strides, keeping something in the tank, the way he'd practiced.

At the end of the first lap, Marcus sprinted. He surged past the chalk line, arms wide, grinning at the fence where the spectators stood, and slowed to a walk with his hands on his head, victorious. Nobody moved. The boy in third place glanced at Coach, confused. Marcus turned around, still breathing hard, and his grin faded.

Ethan passed him, and while he passed him he understood. Marcus hadn't run two laps. He had run one. He'd kicked for the finish a full lap too early, because he'd lost count, and an eight hundred wasn't over at the line, it was only half over. That was the hidden rule of the race, invisible on the chalk, and Ethan could deduce it from Marcus's face alone: the slow dawning horror of a boy doing the math.

The second lap hurt. Ethan's legs burned and his arms pumped and the bee-swatting kid behind him started running again, furious now, closing the gap stride by stride. The fence came up fast. Ethan leaned, drove his knees, crossed the chalk a second time and stumbled onto the grass, gasping.

Marcus finished three seconds later and stood over him, shaking his head. "Two laps," he said. "Nobody told me it was two laps."

"Everybody told you," Ethan wheezed. "You just ran the wrong half first."

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: 1 is not a prime number; mathematicians exclude it so that every whole number has only one way to be written as a product of primes.
story:
Eli typed the last line of his program into the laptop and hit run. On the screen, a prompt blinked: ENTER A NUMBER. He typed 7, and the program printed PRIME. He typed 9, and it printed NOT PRIME. Behind him, Priya leaned over his shoulder, chewing the end of her pen. She had started the coding club's project board, and she wanted every program finished before Friday so the club could vote on which one to demo at the school assembly. "Try one," she said, so he typed 2. PRIME. Then 15. NOT PRIME.

"Try one," Priya said again, and this time she meant the actual number 1. Eli typed it. The screen said PRIME. He frowned at it. One felt like it should be prime. It wasn't even, and nothing divided it except one and itself, which happened to be the same thing. Priya tapped the screen. "That's wrong," she said. "One is not a prime number." She said it the way she said everything, flat and certain, and then she waited, because she wanted him to figure out the rest himself, or at least to try.

Eli could not see why. The rule he had coded, check every possible divisor, worked for 7 and 9 and 15, so the problem was not in the loops. It was in the rule itself, or in the number. He pulled a piece of scrap paper and wrote out products of primes. Six is two times three. Twelve is two times two times three. Fifteen is three times five. Each number came out one way, the same way every time he rewrote it. Then he tried one. One times one times one times one, on and on, and it never stopped. He sat back.

"Mathematicians exclude it," he said slowly, "so that every whole number has only one way to be written as a product of primes." Priya nodded. "That's the line for the board." The whiteboard in the computer lab held the club's rules, and next to it a ballot box made from a shoebox, where members dropped slips voting on the demo program. So far Eli's program had two votes and Marcus's maze game had four.

He added two lines to his code: if the number is one, print NOT PRIME. The school's filter sometimes blocked programs with certain words, but his complied with every rule, so it ran clean. Marcus came by and tested it twice, trying to break it, and the program sat there immune to every trick, printing NOT PRIME for 1 and 0, and PRIME for 13. Eli wrote his program's name on a slip, folded it, and dropped it in the ballot box. "Vote for yourself?" Priya said. "Vote for the math," said Eli, and closed the lid.

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: 2 is the only even prime number, because every larger even number can be divided evenly by 2.
story:
Grandpa's den smelled like pencil shavings and coffee, and the old laptop on his desk made a soft humming sound as Payton typed. She had wanted to build something real all summer, not just play games, and yesterday Grandpa had challenged her: write a program that asks for a number and tells you whether it is prime. "A prime number," he had said, "is only divisible by 1 and itself." That part she understood. The hard part was teaching the computer to check.

Her first idea was simple. Take the number, try dividing it by every smaller number, and if any division came out even, the number was not prime. She wrote a loop with a variable called divisor, ran the program, and typed in 15. "Not prime," the screen said. She punched the air. Then she tried 9, then 25, then 13. All correct. She was feeling like a diplomat negotiating a peace treaty between herself and the machine, and winning.

Then she typed 2.

"Not prime," the screen said.

Payton stared at it. That was wrong. She knew 2 was prime; she had known that since fourth grade. So where was the mistake hiding? She couldn't see it, because the loop was invisible once it ran. All she could see was the answer. She rested her chin on her hand and traced the code with her finger, line by line. "Divide the number by every smaller number," she whispered. Smaller than 2. There was nothing smaller than 2 to divide by, except 1, and dividing by 1 never counted. She exhaled slowly, fogging the corner of the screen. The loop never found anything, so her program reported... not prime? No, wait. If nothing divided evenly, it should say prime. Unless her code had the conditions backwards.

She looked again at her if statement and found it: she had written the print lines in the wrong order, so a number with no divisors got labeled "not prime." That meant every prime would fail, not just 2. She fixed the swap and ran it again. 13: prime. 2: prime. Then she tried 4, and the screen said "Not prime," which was right, because 4 could be divided evenly by 2. So could 6, and 8, and 10, she realized. Two was the only even prime number, the only one standing alone.

The mistakes were starting to feel cumulative, one stacking on another, but so were the fixes. Grandpa appeared in the doorway with two mugs of cocoa. "So?" he asked.

Payton typed 2 one more time and turned the screen toward him. "Prime," it said.

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
knowledge_domain: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
fact: On a distance-time graph, a straight sloping line means the object is moving at a constant speed.
story:
Annabelle crouched at the top of the skate park's smallest ramp with a stopwatch in one hand and a tennis ball in the other. Her science project was due tomorrow morning, and she still needed a graph of the ball's speed. Down at the bottom of the ramp, her friend Dez held a tape measure stretched along the smooth concrete, drumming his fingers on his knee. "Can we hurry?" he said. "I signed up for the beginners' trick clinic at four, and if I miss it, I lose my spot."

"Ten more minutes," Annabelle said. "I promise." She had marked the ramp every meter with chalk, and her plan was simple: roll the ball, time it, write down where it was at each second. But she didn't just want numbers. She wanted to know what the ball's motion looked like, and you couldn't see speed itself, only see where the ball was and when. She wondered what shape all those little measurements would make if she connected them.

She rolled the ball and clicked the stopwatch, calling out positions as it passed each chalk mark. They ran three trials, then sat on the edge of the half-pipe and plotted the points on graph paper. Annabelle drew the axis for distance and the axis for time, then connected the dots. She sat back. "Look at this. It's almost perfectly straight." The line climbed steadily up the page, like a ramp drawn in ink. Was that normal, or had they measured wrong? She had expected some wobbly curve, something messy, because the ball was speeding along and then slowing and she couldn't watch it closely.

Dez leaned over her shoulder, but his eyes kept drifting to the older skaters carving the big bowl. "Is that bad?" he asked. Annabelle shook her head slowly. "No. A straight sloping line means it's going at a constant speed." She tried it in her head. The ball on the smooth concrete covered the same distance every second, so every point sat evenly along one line. She rolled the ball again on the rough gravel by the fence, plotted those points, and got a line that bent and flattened. The concrete ramp made the straight line; the gravel did not.

"See? Same ball, different surface, different shape," she said, tapping the two graphs side by side. "Mr. Okafor will ask me how I know it's constant speed, and now I can justify my answer with both graphs, not just a guess." Dez stood up and grabbed his board. "Good, because I have to justify skipping my clinic to my grandpa, and he already thinks skateboarding will bankrupt his pension if I break another helmet." Annabelle laughed and packed her papers into her backpack.

At the gate she paused, looking back at the empty ramp, already wondering whether the ball would make a straighter line on the bigger ramp, or whether a steeper line meant a faster ball. "Tomorrow after school," she said to Dez, "want to help me with one more trial?" Dez balanced his board on one hand and grinned. "Only if I get to roll it off the tall ramp first."

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: In the United States, Feeding America is a nationwide network of more than 200 food banks.
story:
On Saturday morning Lucy stood in her kitchen, staring at the permission slip her mom had signed the night before. It said she would volunteer at the community food bank from nine until noon, and the words alone were enough to intimidate her. She had never been, and she pictured a giant warehouse full of strangers who all knew exactly what to do except her.

"Take the muffins," her mom said, sliding a paper bag across the counter. "Ask for Mr. Okafor. And Lucy, if the neighbor's cat comes near the birds again, shoo him off, okay? That animal is pure predatory instinct in a fur coat."

The cat was already crouched under the feeder, tail twitching, eyes fixed on the sparrows. Lucy banged the door on her way out and he fled, offended.

The food bank turned out to be smaller than she'd imagined, more like a big garage than a warehouse, with shelves of canned beans and rice rising to the ceiling. Mr. Okafor handed her a clipboard. "You're on inventory. Count the pasta, write the number, don't guess."

A boy about her age, Deshawn, was already at the next shelf, counting fast. "I'm here every weekend," he said. "My grandma used to come here for groceries. Now I want to work here someday, for real. Paycheck and everything."

Mid-morning, a truck backed up to the loading door, and Lucy noticed a logo on its side, a bowl with a fork. "That's the second truck today with that same picture," she said. "But the first one had Dallas plates and this one's local. How can they both have it?"

Deshawn shrugged. Mr. Okafor kept unloading. Lucy chewed her pencil. Same logo, different cities. It couldn't be a coincidence, and it couldn't be that one company owned trucks everywhere. Her guess: it had to be some kind of network, one name covering lots of separate food banks.

She found the answer on a poster by the office door. "Feeding America," she read slowly. "It's a nationwide network of more than 200 food banks." She counted the words twice. More than two hundred. Dallas, her town, and probably everywhere else.

"So we're connected to Dallas," she told Deshawn.

"That's why the trucks look alike," he said. "Huh. Whole country's in on it." He went back to counting, but he was grinning.

At noon, Lucy carried out the empty muffin bag and found the neighbor's cat back under the feeder, frozen like a statue. The sparrows' calm was an illusion; they hadn't seen him yet. She clapped her hands and they scattered upward, safe.

"See you next Saturday," Deshawn called from the door. Lucy waved and walked home, already planning to sign up again.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Día de los Muertos, celebrated in Mexico mainly on November 1 and 2, honors family members who have died with home altars called ofrendas.
story:
The pavilion at Riverside Park had been decorated since morning, and Gabriel arrived with his mother, his tía Rosa, and a plastic bag holding one sugar skull that had already lost an arm. A banner over the tables read "Día de los Muertos, November 1 and 2." His tía had explained in the car, more than once, that in Mexico these were the days for honoring family members who had died, and that families built altars in their homes for it. Gabriel mostly cared about one thing: he was supposed to add his grandfather's photo to the community altar today, and he had left the photo in the printer tray at home.

The altar stood at the end of the longest table. A girl from his class, Marisol, was arranging frames on it. "It's called an ofrenda," she said when he stood there too long without doing anything. "My great-grandfather goes here." She set down a photo of a man in a straw hat holding a radio.

Gabriel checked his mother's phone for the picture he wanted, the one of his grandfather laughing at a barbecue. The battery bar was red, then the screen went black. He borrowed Tía Rosa's phone, but the photo had never been sent to her. He had a copy only at home, and home was a twenty-minute walk.

While he decided what to do, he noticed something odd. The candles on the ofrenda kept going out. Marisol relit one, and it died again within a minute. An old man nearby blamed the candles themselves, saying they were cheap, but Gabriel crouched and watched. The flames all bent in the same direction, toward the lake. When a group of people walked past the open side of the pavilion, the flames accelerated sideways, flickered hard, and went out. It wasn't the candles. Wind was funneling between the two support posts on the north side, and the candles sat directly in that channel.

He tested it by holding a single candle near the posts, then behind the stacked pan de muerto at the center of the table. At the posts it guttered. Behind the bread, the flame stood still. He and Marisol moved the candleholders to the sheltered middle of the ofrenda, and none of them went out for the rest of the afternoon. The old man gave a small nod, as if he had suspected wind all along.

Then Gabriel ran home. He got the photo, ran back through the falling leaves, out of breath, and slid it into an empty frame Marisol had saved. He placed it beside her great-grandfather with the radio.

When his mother saw it, she said, "He would have liked being next to somebody who loved music that much."

Gabriel straightened the frame so his grandfather's grin faced the whole park.

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: Chlorine bleach must never be mixed with cleaners containing ammonia, because together they release chloramine, a toxic gas.
story:
Alexis stood in the laundry aisle of Hillcrest Grocery with a crumpled list in one hand and a grudge in the other. Last week her favorite hoodie had come out of the wash the size of a hamster sweater, and her mom had said, maybe next time you let me handle it. No. Alexis was going to handle it. She was going to become a fully competent laundry person, and the hoodie incident would be remembered as history.

"Detergent, stain spray, bleach," she read off the list. "For whites. And the ammonia spray for the bathroom, it's on sale." She grabbed a jug of chlorine bleach, then reached for the ammonia cleaner, planning to stack them in the cart like good friends.

Then she flipped the bottles over and read the backs, because her science teacher had made them do that once with a bottle of drain opener and it had been mildly terrifying. The bleach label said never mix with cleaners containing ammonia. The ammonia label said the same thing in bolder letters, like it was yelling in print. Together they release chloramine, a toxic gas.

Alexis held the two bottles at arm's length from each other, as if they might leap. "You two are not carpooling," she informed them. She set the bleach in the front of the cart and the ammonia spray way down in the back, under the paper towels, where they couldn't even see each other.
